<reason>Both sides argued tightly and stayed on the motion. CON's strongest live route was mechanistic: outcomes contracts cannot recapture premiums and fills already paid, and a mandate removes the indication-level walk-away. PRO's strongest route was structural and moral: the "hard no" CON defends has been exercised for years without moving prices because it is aimed at the patient, not the seller; the only no that has ever moved manufacturers is brand-level exclusion inside a large negotiated market, which the motion preserves. PRO's pressure questions exposed that CON's remaining principle distinguishing obesity from diabetes reduces to scale, and CON never named a case where fragmented refusal beat pooled negotiation—its A2 largely pivoted to brand-preference, which is PRO's own mechanism. PRO also collected CON's concessions (drugs work, molecule insured for diabetes, outcomes deals exist) into a decisive frame: the last principle is "too many people have this disease." CON's closing retort ("scale is not cruelty"; "fills paid first") was sharp and kept it competitive, and PRO paid a real execution cost with two clipped turns, but PRO answered CON's Q1 directly (holdouts lose the shelf to competitors) while CON's answer to PRO's Q2 evaded. PRO made the decision easier to render.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's inversion of the leverage argument ([B2.2], [B4.3]): insurers already hold the "hard no," prices held anyway, and that no falls on the sick patient rather than the manufacturer—CON never produced a case of indication-level refusal lowering net price, leaving its spine argument reframed as patient denial rather than buyer leverage.</best_rebuttal>
